issues.description: The supplied SAS workflow reads 31 distinct external input products/files: native CSMAR statement/market/audit modules, Datago sentiment data, author-manual workbooks and crosswalks, and a yearbook-derived workbook. None are in this ZIP. Product-specific field names are traced from the source, but exact source contracts, IDs, formats, period coverage, and compatible routes remain unresolved; catalog misses do not establish absent access or licensing.

The datasheet describes Datago data for 1998–2014, while SAS filters the imported news data through year<=2016. The final panel is through 2014; the incoming CSV encoding, source-vendor field/sentiment contract, and reason for the extra two years are unresolved. This input contract is distinct from the known GBK encoding of the SAS source code.
The frozen SAS empty-session probes fail with a TKELS initialization error before establishing a SAS session. This does not show that a SAS license or any product component is absent.

The workflow requires SAS/ETS PROC EXPAND, SAS/STAT PROC REG/GLM/LOGISTIC/SURVEYSELECT, Excel/CSV import, and Stata DTA export. Product/component availability and DBMS=EXCEL compatibility on the local SAS platform are unverified.

The source bytes are verified as GBK and contain Chinese literals and a Chinese Datago filename. A GBK-to-UTF-8 or other session-compatible conversion on a working copy is deterministic preparation; round-trip-check the literals and path and leave the original unchanged. SAS startup and session/component availability are assessed separately under I-SAS-STARTUP and the SAS software records.

Both programs hard-code Windows E: paths. The SAS path tree distinguishes the richlist project root from daily, weekly, and monthly CSMAR libraries, and Stata reads outputs under the project root. A consistent writable host-visible relative or [redacted-path-2e4a1c6a9a42] mapping has not been prepared.
The exact ttable2 command required by the Table 4 branch was not found in the checked default/shared Stata adopaths; no distribution/source was verified.

evidence.description: Datasheet documents manual Hurun list collection and the named 2008–2014 web sources.
evidence.quote:
a) The Hurun Rich List data
       The Rich List data from 1999 to 2007 were collected from Hoogewerf and
       Dongfang (2008). The Rich List data from 2008 to 2014 were collected from the
       following websites:
       http://finance.sina.com.cn/g/20081007/10365362391.shtml
       http://finance.sina.com.cn/g/20091013/10256831606.shtml
       http://finance.sina.com.cn/focus/hurun_2010/
       http://money.163.com/special/2011hurun/
       http://finance.sina.com.cn/focus/2012hurun/
       http://finance.sina.com.cn/focus/2013hrbfb/
       http://finance.sina.com.cn/focus/hurunbaif/
       From the above sources, we manually collect the identities of the wealthy people
       or families and their rankings on the list. Based on information from firms’ IPO
       prospectuses, public-listing announcements, annual reports, and the Web, we then
       determine the public firms that are ultimately controlled by the entrepreneurs of
       interest.
       The above data were last updated in September 2015.

evidence.description: Datasheet documents CSMAR and manual auditor data, Datago press data, CSMAR financial/share data, ownership, and yearbook corruption data.
evidence.quote:
b) Signatory auditor and their demographic data
       The data for the identities of auditor and audit opinions were first downloaded from
       the China Stock Market and Accounting Research Database (CSMAR), and if
       missing, we searched the client companies’ annual reports or the database for
       Chinese public accountants at http://cmis.cicpa.org.cn. The data for auditor loca-
       tions were manually collected from audit reports and/or client companies’ annual
       reports.
       The above data were last updated in June 2016.
   c) Press coverage data
       We obtain the press coverage data for the period of 1998–2014 from Datago, a data
       vendor specialized in textual analyses of Chinese news reports on public companies

                                            1

       in China. Based on 15 million some news articles published since 1998, Datago
       uses a machine-learning algorithm to determine sentence-level sentiment leaning.
       The above data were last updated in January 2018.
   d) Financial statement and share price data
       These data, in machine readable form, were downloaded from the CSMAR. The
       data were downloaded for multiple times.
       The latest date for downloading the data used in this study is May 2019.
   e) Ownership structure data
       We primarily used the ownership data in the CSMAR and manually collected the
       data for observations with missing values.
       These data were downloaded and collected in June 2017.
   f) Regional corruption data
       We obtained these data from Procuratorial Yearbooks of China in January 2016.

evidence.description: SAS reads the CSMAR balance sheet, income statement, cash flow statement, and FI_T10 industry table and constructs the base panel.
SAS imports TRD_Co to construct listing year, industry, and market type.
SAS imports two hand-collected opening-balance workbooks and uses them to supplement missing prior financial values.
SAS derives control variables and NOA from statement items and opening/closing balance inputs.
SAS consumes six daily-price year shards, CG_Capchg share counts, and FR_T6 for the pre-1999 Tobin Q values.
SAS constructs weekly industry returns from TRD_Week fields and creates lead/lag weekly series.
SAS reads TRD_WeekCM market returns, merges them with weekly stock returns, and estimates synweek.
SAS imports press sentiment fields and builds firm-year news, negative-news, positive-news, and sentiment-share measures.
SAS imports RS_Capc to create SEO and its one-year lead.
SAS imports FN_Fn020 fixed-asset footnote fields for 2007 onward.
SAS reads the old CSMAR balance-sheet table to fill fixed-asset values through 2006.
SAS estimates industry-year discretionary accruals using annual financial data and a winsor macro.
SAS imports STK_Violation_Main and defines the sanction outcome from Chinese violation and supervisor fields.
SAS imports SOE.xlsx and derives lagged SOE flags.
SAS imports FIN_Audit and a separate exchange-rate workbook to derive audit opinions and converted fees.
SAS joins CSMAR audit/CPA and manually collected auditor-location records.
SAS imports manually collected listed-firm registration provinces.
SAS reads three Corrupt.xlsx sheets, transposes year columns, and derives provincial corruption measures.
SAS imports FN_Fn025 impairment data and derives components used in effective tax rate.
SAS uses old balance-sheet fields and beginning values to extend impairment measures for early years.
SAS imports SPT_Trdchg and derives the ST variable.
SAS imports the 1999–2012 Hurun file and combines ranks with the author-coded identity fields.
SAS imports the code_namecode crosswalk and builds rich/control samples from listing dates and identity matches.
SAS exports reg1_main.dta and saves the rich, control, and findata intermediate datasets.
SAS uses the Hurun and rich_share_pos inputs for Table 1 wealth, cash-flow-right, and executive-position analyses.
SAS builds the exact-size matched sample and exports reg2_match_TA.dta.
SAS builds the exact-size-and-ROA matched sample and exports reg3_match_TA_ROA.dta.
SAS winsorizes the matching pool, estimates PSM, matches without replacement, and exports reg4_match_PSM.dta.
SAS creates the seeded placebo listing sample and exports reg5_placebo.dta.
SAS combines both Hurun files and the firm mapping to create the non-top-200 falsification sample and export reg6_falsify.dta.
Stata sets the project directory and consumes reg1_main.dta first.

evidence.quote:
A. Predicting the listing of firms’ controlling owners by public-firm data

In section 3.1 of the paper, we contend that the outsiders, such as the auditors, cannot easily predict whether
the owners of the clients will be included in the Rich List because the development of the private sector in
China does not rely much on the country’s stock market (Allen et al. 2005). We use data for non-state firms
in the A-share market to verify this point empirically.

       For each year, we identify two groups of firms: (a) those controlled by the billionaires who are first
ranked among the top 200 on the list, and (b) firms where the controlling owners are never ranked as one
of the 200 richest people by the end of our sample period. Actual Listing is an indicator for observations in
the first group defined above. We use variable Wealth, defined as Ln(market value of firms of interest at
the end of August × the percentage of cash-flow rights of their ultimate controlling owners), Leverage
(financial leverage), ROA (operating income divided by total assets), Ln(TAST) (natural logarithm of total
assets), and industry and year fixed effects, to predict Actual Listing.

       In the logistic model results reported in panel A of Table A1, we find that Wealth, Leverage, and ROA
are loaded with statistically significant coefficients, and pseudo-R2 of 0.233 also suggests the model fits the
data reasonably well. To assess the model’s predictive performance, we convert the regression model to
binary classification in panel B. Specifically, we set the threshold probability as the percentage of Actual

evidence.description: The online appendix describes three matching methods and a separate covariate-comparison table.
evidence.quote:
B. Comparing the treatment and matched control firms

In section 4.2.3 of the paper, we use three matching methods to identify control observations: (a) Exact
matching based on firm size [Ln(TAST)] in T – 1; (b) Exact matching based on firm size [Ln(TAST)] and
profitability (ROA) in T – 1; and (c) The propensity-score matching (PSM) based on a propensity score, P-
Score, derived from a logistic model that predicts whether an observation will experience its first rich listing
in T by the relevant covariates in T – 1. For the above three matching methods, we report the mean values
of the covariates between the treatment and matched control firms, and the t-tests for the between-group
differences in mean values in Table A2. The differences in the matching variables are statistically
insignificant under the three methods, implying the matching is generally successful.
